title: Commodity plastics returned to monomers at a cost and energy below virgin production

concept.text: The proposed innovation is an industrial process that turns discarded polyethylene (PE) and polypropylene (PP) into recoverable ethylene and propylene, the small molecules used to manufacture these plastics, while consuming less total energy and costing less than comparable production from virgin fossil feedstocks. Its intended feed is real mixed postconsumer waste, with measured additives and contamination. Achieving this would require integrating selective chemical conversion with waste preparation, continuous operation, catalyst management and product purification. The supplied studies demonstrate parts of that capability, but do not establish the complete process.

The central chemical challenge is controlling the breakdown of the strong carbon–carbon backbones of polyolefins so that useful light olefins dominate the products. Simply converting plastic into a mixture of smaller hydrocarbons is insufficient: the desired ethylene and propylene must also be recovered in a form suitable for making new polymers. Returning mixed PE and PP to this shared monomer pool would support circular production without requiring each waste polymer to produce exclusively its own original monomer.

significance.text: The cited polyolefin study reports that polyolefins account for more than half of plastic waste. Selectively recovering their monomers would therefore address a large materials stream whose carbon–carbon backbones make chemical recycling difficult. If recovered ethylene and propylene were sufficiently pure, affordable and available at adequate throughput, waste polyolefins could compete as feedstocks for new PE and PP. The direct consequence would be an economically credible route to closed-loop production of these polymers.

Impact synthesis: the revolutionary feature would be changing the economics of an abundant waste stream, making discarded material a competitive source of primary chemical building blocks. The analogy to inexpensive steel transforming construction expresses the possible importance of a change in material cost and supply; it is not a prediction that adoption would follow the same path. Large-scale displacement of fossil feedstocks would additionally depend on collection, sorting, plant capacity, product purification and integration with existing chemical manufacturing.

The scope is substantial but bounded. Polyester methanolysis uses different chemistry, and the cited polyester work leaves PE and PP largely unreacted. Success with mixed PE and PP would not by itself establish solutions for textiles, composites, thermosets or PVC. This proposal also makes no claim of universal quantitative yields, zero energy input or zero by-products. Those stronger claims are unnecessary to its significance.

The thermodynamic distinction matters: the polyolefin study's supplementary model finds full conversion of PE into ethylene and propylene theoretically feasible above 673 K under its assumptions. The supplied evidence therefore does not justify a blanket claim that 100% conversion or yield necessarily violates thermodynamics. That model also does not establish a practical, zero-energy recycling process or extend to every polymer.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability within the supplied demonstrations is sustained conversion of representative mixed postconsumer PE and PP into ethylene and propylene as the major recovered products, with a complete energy and cost balance below comparable virgin monomer production. The studies include waste-feed tests, gram-scale conversion and short continuous feeding, so the gap cannot accurately be described as an absence of all work beyond clean, tiny batches. Their results nevertheless leave a substantial distance between laboratory selectivity and an integrated industrial process.

Maintaining selectivity as throughput and operating duration increase is a concrete engineering challenge. The high-yield laboratory process uses independently heated stages and substantial catalyst quantities relative to the polymer charge. Its lower combined yield in a one-gram experiment and its short continuous-feeding demonstration make scale-dependent performance and long-term catalyst behavior important questions. These observations identify what requires demonstration; they do not prove that scale-up will fail.

Contaminant tolerance is another specific barrier. The supplementary experiments report that strongly basic nitrogen-containing additives substantially impair catalytic activity. Separate waste-polyolefin tests do not establish tolerance of arbitrary mixtures, variable additive packages or other polymers at packaging-waste concentrations. A useful process must either tolerate a declared range of these materials or remove them with pretreatment whose losses, energy use and costs are included.

Recovering suitable monomers is part of the unsolved integration problem. Reactor yield alone does not establish the quantity, purity or cost of products available for repolymerization. The cited preliminary economics exclude subsequent product separation and compare against a waste-PE pyrolysis route. They therefore do not establish the proposed advantage over virgin ethylene and propylene production. Catalyst preparation and regeneration, thermal requirements, pretreatment and separation must be assessed together on a comparable boundary.

current_state.text: On 14 October 2025, Tianrui Bi, Yinlin Chen, Longfei Lin and colleagues reported a kinetic decoupling–recoupling process in Nature Chemical Engineering. They describe conventional catalytic cracking of PE as limiting combined ethylene and propylene yields to below 25%, and report up to 79% carbon molar yield with their process. The optimized experiment used 100 mg of high-density polyethylene, 12.5 mg of first-stage catalyst with a 260–300 °C temperature program, and 100 mg total second-stage catalyst at 540 °C. This establishes a substantial laboratory selectivity advance under specified conditions.

The same study goes beyond clean-resin batch experiments. It reports separate waste-polyolefin tests, an eight-hour continuous-feeding experiment at 0.1 g per hour with around 75% combined ethylene and propylene selectivity, and conversion of one gram of PE within four hours with a 57% combined ethylene and propylene yield. The continuous-run selectivity is a different metric from the optimized 79% carbon molar yield and should not be treated as interchangeable with it. These remain laboratory demonstrations rather than evidence of sustained commodity-scale production.

The study's preliminary economic analysis uses waste-PE pyrolysis as its comparator and omits subsequent product separation costs. It does not demonstrate a complete cost or energy advantage over virgin monomer production. The supplied review describes complete retained main-article and supplementary text for this study, allowing these distinctions to be grounded in more than an abstract; this does not imply independent inspection of original figure images or additional documents.

On 8 September 2025, Julia B. Curley, Yuanzhe Liang, Jason S. DesVeaux and colleagues, including Beckham and Knauer, reported mild methanolysis of mixed polyesters in one reactor in Nature Chemical Engineering. The accessible abstract identifies PET, PLA, PBAT and PBS and reports high monomer yields, kilogram-scale work and integrated separations. This represents more extensive scale-up and separations integration in the cited work, for a different polymer family. The supplementary evidence identifies PE and PP in the unreacted residue, directly limiting any inference that the process also solves polyolefin conversion.

Access to the polyester main article in the supplied review was limited to a subscription preview containing the substantive abstract; its full main text was not available there. A complete retained supplementary document supports the narrower observation about unreacted polyolefins. The reported kilogram scale-up and separations should therefore be understood as claims supported by the accessible abstract, without implying that all main-paper experimental details were inspected.

Evidence limitation: the earlier research attributes greater-than-90% yields of propylene, or propylene and isobutylene, with an ethylene co-feed to a 2024 Science paper identified by DOI 10.1126/science.adq7316. No retained text of that paper accompanies the supplied review. Its numerical yield, detailed conditions and claimed earlier capture followed by a failed fetch cannot be verified from this record. This is a limitation of the available evidence, not evidence that the reported result is false.

Temporal limitation: the supplied evidence documents the dated 2025 achievements above, but contains no bounded freshness search establishing the state of the entire field on 1 November 2026. It supports the conclusion that these particular studies do not demonstrate the combined industrial capability. It does not establish that no other process had achieved it by that date.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: operate a continuous unit at a declared throughput on real mixed PE and PP waste for thousands of hours, producing ethylene and propylene as the major recovered products. Measure and disclose the feed's polymer composition, additives and contaminants, and test stated ranges representative of packaging waste. Report startup, interruptions, catalyst replacement or regeneration and performance over time. Thousands of hours is a proposed durability threshold for this record, not an established consensus standard.
completion_criteria.label: Mixed PE/PP waste continuously yields ethylene/propylene for thousands of hours

completion_criteria.text: Proposed product and accounting requirements: publish carbon and mass balances, distinguish conversion, selectivity, reactor yield and recovered-product yield, and report product purity suitable for repolymerization. Demonstrating production of new PE and PP from the recovered monomer streams would strengthen the closed-loop claim. By-products, residues, material losses and any external reactant or co-feed contributions should be quantified so that apparent monomer recovery is not confused with carbon supplied from elsewhere.
completion_criteria.label: Publish complete carbon and mass balances with repolymerization-grade monomer purity

completion_criteria.text: Proposed comparative requirement: show lower total energy use and cost than naphtha cracking on an explicit, comparable system boundary and matched ethylene/propylene product basis. Include feed preparation, catalyst preparation and regeneration, heating and cooling, product separation and waste treatment. Disclose assumptions about waste acquisition, plant scale, energy prices and co-product allocation. Any broader claim to outperform virgin production should also identify which alternative virgin feedstocks and production routes were compared.
completion_criteria.label: Lower total energy and cost than comparable naphtha cracking

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: provide operating procedures and data sufficient for independent replication, repeat the demonstration across multiple waste lots, and disclose the feed compositions and contaminant levels at which performance deteriorates. Independent verification of balances and recovered-product quality would make the claim more convincing. Finite tests would establish demonstrated breadth across those conditions, not literal universality across all plastic waste. A near-80% laboratory carbon yield on clean resin alone would not satisfy these integrated criteria.
completion_criteria.label: Enable independent replication across waste lots and disclose feed limits

related_concepts.text: Roster synthesis: CHEMREV-07, fossil-competitive multicarbon chemicals from CO2 and water, shares the goal of replacing fossil feedstocks through competitive chemical production. CHEMREV-13 recovers carbon already embodied in polymers, whereas CHEMREV-07 builds chemicals from CO2 and water. The two could complement each other in a materials economy, but progress in one does not demonstrate the other's feedstock, energy or economic requirements.

Roster synthesis: CHEMREV-05, enzyme-level catalysts on request for arbitrary reactions, could help discover catalysts for selective polyolefin conversion. CHEMREV-01, realistic prediction of chemical outcomes before experiment, could help anticipate reaction products and contaminant effects. CHEMREV-13 requires effective chemistry for a bounded industrial task; it does not require either general catalyst design or broadly predictive chemical modeling to be solved.

Roster synthesis: CHEMREV-06, mild nitrogen fixation competitive with Haber–Bosch, and CHEMREV-12, selective methane-to-methanol conversion, share the need to combine selectivity, useful throughput, durability and complete process economics. CHEMREV-11 instead targets functionalization of a chosen unactivated C–H bond in a complex molecule. These entries concern distinct chemical transformations: success in polyolefin backbone cleavage and monomer recovery would not establish nitrogen fixation, methane oxidation or general site-selective functionalization.

Roster synthesis: CHEMREV-04 concerns practical synthesis of arbitrary stable molecules; CHEMREV-09 concerns phase-pure synthesis of arbitrary designed crystalline solids; and CHEMREV-10 concerns macroscopic matter with specified atomic arrangements. CHEMREV-13 has a narrower output objective: bulk recovery of a few monomers. CHEMREV-02, synthetic chemical evolution, CHEMREV-03, an ambient-pressure room-temperature superconductor, and CHEMREV-08, an aviation-relevant air-breathing battery, address separate capabilities with no direct dependency established by the supplied material.

Polyester methanolysis is a closely related circular-materials approach outside the supplied roster. It shares the ambition of recovering useful monomers from waste, and the cited study contributes evidence about mixed feeds, scale-up and separations. Its different polymer chemistry and the persistence of PE and PP in its residue preserve the distinction from CHEMREV-13 rather than resolving or replacing it.

change_log.change: Preserved CHEMREV-13 and its title while defining the target as an integrated, still-hypothetical PE/PP-to-monomer process.
change_log.reason: The review supports the concept's coherence and laboratory foundations without demonstrating its complete industrial performance.

change_log.change: Replaced the clean-polymer-only framing with the documented waste-polyolefin tests, one-gram experiment and eight-hour continuous-feeding experiment.
change_log.reason: The earlier account understated the range of demonstrated feeds and operating modes.

change_log.change: Specified the optimized 260–300 °C first-stage program, 540 °C second stage and catalyst quantities; distinguished 79% carbon molar yield, roughly 75% continuous-run selectivity and 57% gram-scale yield.
change_log.reason: These conditions and metrics describe different experiments and cannot be combined into one performance claim.

change_log.change: Identified the economic comparator as waste-PE pyrolysis and retained the exclusion of subsequent product separation.
change_log.reason: The preliminary analysis does not establish a complete advantage over virgin monomer production.

change_log.change: Grounded contaminant concerns in the reported inhibition by strongly basic nitrogen-containing additives.
change_log.reason: This supplies a concrete scientific barrier rather than an unspecified concern about dirty waste.

change_log.change: Replaced the broad plastic-production share assertion with the reported greater-than-50% share of plastic waste for polyolefins.
change_log.reason: The supplied source supports the waste-category statement, not the original production-share wording.

change_log.change: Made industrial deployment conditional and retained the inexpensive-steel analogy as an explicitly interpretive comparison.
change_log.reason: Competitive chemistry could enable circular production, but collection, throughput, purification and integration still govern adoption.

change_log.change: Added the polyester study's reported kilogram scale-up and integrated separations, its unreacted PE/PP residue and its partial main-article access.
change_log.reason: These details clarify both its useful progress and its chemical and evidentiary boundaries.

change_log.change: Qualified the optional Science yield and retrieval-history claims instead of treating them as verified or false.
change_log.reason: No corresponding retained article text or retrieval artifacts were supplied.

change_log.change: Removed the implication of a universal thermodynamic prohibition on quantitative conversion.
change_log.reason: The supplied PE model permits full conversion above 673 K under its assumptions, while establishing no universal zero-energy process.

change_log.change: Expanded the proposed completion criteria to include throughput, recovered-product purity, complete balances, reproducibility and explicit comparison boundaries.
change_log.reason: These additions make the intended industrial capability assessable without presenting proposed thresholds as established standards.

change_log.change: Limited claims about the remaining gap to the supplied studies and added explicit temporal uncertainty.
change_log.reason: The record contains no freshness search establishing field-wide absence of the capability on 1 November 2026.

unresolved_issues: Whether any process outside the supplied studies had achieved the combined industrial capability by 1 November 2026 remains unresolved.
The 2024 Science paper's greater-than-90% yield, precise yield basis, co-feed accounting and claimed retrieval history remain unverified in the supplied record.
Long-duration catalyst performance, regeneration requirements and tolerance of representative mixed packaging waste have not been established by the supplied demonstrations.
A complete comparison with virgin monomer production, including product separation and a matched product basis, remains unavailable here.
The polyester main article was available only as a subscription preview in the supplied review; its full experimental account was not inspected there.
The proposed throughput, acceptable contamination range, monomer-purity specifications and durability threshold require concrete selection for an actual demonstration; they are not settled standards.

brief.title: Making new plastics from waste more cheaply than from oil
possible: Discarded polyethylene and polypropylene, common packaging plastics, could become raw materials for new plastics. A factory would turn mixed waste into ethylene and propylene—the small molecules used to make these plastics—using less energy and costing less than making them from fresh fossil feedstocks.
why: These plastics account for more than half of plastic waste. Recovering their building blocks cheaply would give manufacturers an economically competitive source of material and support a loop from discarded plastic back to new plastic.

sources.who: Tianrui Bi, Yinlin Chen, Longfei Lin and colleagues
sources.showed: Their laboratory process converted up to 79% of polyethylene's carbon into ethylene and propylene by controlling reactions in separately heated stages. They also tested waste plastics and continuous feeding.
sources.quote: Here we address this challenge with a kinetic decoupling–recoupling (KDRC) strategy, achieving yields of ethylene and propylene up to 79% from PE conversion using a tandem reactor with dual zeolite catalysts.
sources.cited_for: Controlled chemical breakdown can direct much of polyethylene's carbon into the desired building blocks.
sources.not_established: The work does not establish sustained industrial production with full purification, energy use and costs below fossil-based production.

sources.who: Julia B. Curley, Yuanzhe Liang, Jason S. DesVeaux and colleagues
sources.showed: They broke down mixed polyesters, a different family of plastics, at kilogram scale and separated the building blocks. They made new PET, a polyester, with properties comparable to material made from commercial ingredients.
sources.quote: PET synthesized from monomers isolated from postconsumer materials showed comparable mechanical and thermal properties to PET from commercial monomers.
sources.cited_for: For another plastic family, chemical recycling has combined larger batches, purification and production of new plastic.
sources.not_established: The process leaves polyethylene and polypropylene largely unreacted, so it does not solve their recycling.

shown: Bi and colleagues have demonstrated laboratory conversion of polyethylene into its useful building blocks, including waste-plastic tests and continuous feeding for eight hours. Curley and colleagues have integrated breakdown and purification at larger scale for polyesters.
missing: Sustained operation on representative mixed packaging waste, with additives and contamination measured.
Recovery of building blocks pure enough for new plastic, with all incoming and outgoing material accounted for.
A complete energy and cost advantage over comparable fossil-based production, including cleaning, heating, purification and waste treatment.
Long-term performance of catalysts, the materials that drive the reactions, including their restoration or replacement.

milestones.label: Mixed waste keeps yielding the desired building blocks
milestones.explanation: A continuous unit would have to process real mixed polyethylene and polypropylene waste for thousands of hours, recovering mainly ethylene and propylene. This would test durability under declared waste conditions.

milestones.label: Pure building blocks and complete material accounting
milestones.explanation: Measurements would have to account for all material and carbon, including added reactants, and establish purity suitable for making new plastic. This would distinguish usable recovery from reactor output alone.

milestones.label: Lower total energy use and cost than fossil production
milestones.explanation: A full comparison would have to beat cracking naphtha, a fossil feedstock, on energy and cost for matched products. Including preparation, catalysts, purification and waste treatment would establish the economic advantage.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce results across different waste lots
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce the process across waste lots, with operating details and failure limits disclosed. This would establish how broadly the results hold.

uncertain: The appropriate operating scale, acceptable contamination range, product-purity targets and durability threshold remain unsettled.
It remains unclear how the share of plastic recovered as useful building blocks changes as throughput rises.
